title: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks
author: Rebecca Skloot
one_line_takeaway: Cells taken without consent from a poor Black woman in 1951 became one of medicine's most important tools, while her family went decades without knowing — a story about science's debts and the people it forgets.
synopsis:
In 1951 Henrietta Lacks, a Black tobacco farmer from southern Virginia and mother of five living in Baltimore, went to Johns Hopkins Hospital with cervical cancer. Without her knowledge, a doctor took a sample of her tumour and passed it to the lab of George Gey, who had been trying for years to grow human cells in culture. Her cells — which became known as HeLa — grew and divided indefinitely, becoming the first immortal human cell line. Henrietta died that October at the age of thirty-one.

HeLa cells went on to help develop the polio vaccine and advance research into cancer, viruses, gene mapping, in vitro fertilisation and much more; they were mass-produced, sold and shipped around the world. Yet Henrietta's family did not learn her cells were alive until more than twenty years later, when researchers contacted them for blood samples, and they never shared in the profits while many of them could not afford health insurance.

Rebecca Skloot braids three stories: Henrietta's life and death, the scientific and commercial life of HeLa, and her own decade-long effort to earn the trust of the Lacks family — especially Henrietta's daughter Deborah, who longed to know who her mother and her lost sister Elsie had been. Along the way the book examines consent, race and medical exploitation, and who owns the tissues taken from our bodies.

ideas.title: Consent and the ownership of tissue
ideas.summary: Henrietta's cells were taken and used without her knowledge or consent, which was common practice at the time. The book questions whether people should control, or profit from, tissues taken from their bodies — a question the law has largely answered no.
ideas.evidence: In Moore v. Regents of the University of California (1990), the California Supreme Court ruled that John Moore had no property rights over cells from his removed spleen that his doctor had turned into a profitable cell line.

ideas.title: Race, poverty and medicine
ideas.summary: Henrietta's story sits within a long history of medical research exploiting Black Americans and the poor, which shaped her family's deep distrust of doctors and scientists.
ideas.evidence: Johns Hopkins had public wards for Black patients in the segregation era; the Tuskegee syphilis study left Black men untreated for decades; Chester Southam injected HeLa cells into patients without informed consent to study cancer immunity.

ideas.title: The science of HeLa
ideas.summary: HeLa cells were remarkably hardy and fast-growing, making them the workhorse of twentieth-century cell biology and launching an industry of cell culture.
ideas.evidence: George Gey gave the cells freely to other researchers; HeLa was used to test the polio vaccine, with a production facility at the Tuskegee Institute; the cells were later found to have contaminated many other cell lines, as Stanley Gartler reported in 1966.

ideas.title: A person erased behind a cell line
ideas.summary: For decades Henrietta was reduced to an abbreviation, her identity misreported or forgotten, while her cells became famous.
ideas.evidence: Her name was often given as 'Helen Lane' or 'Helen Larson'; Skloot first heard of HeLa in a community college biology class where the instructor knew almost nothing about the woman behind it.

ideas.title: The family's cost
ideas.summary: The Lacks family learned of HeLa only by accident, received little explanation and no compensation, and struggled with poverty, illness and confusion about what had been done to their mother.
ideas.evidence: In 1973 researchers took blood from family members to study HeLa contamination without clearly explaining why, leaving them believing they were being tested for cancer. Henrietta's daughter Elsie, who had epilepsy, died at the Hospital for the Negro Insane in Crownsville.

ideas.title: Deborah's search and the writer's responsibility
ideas.summary: Skloot's relationship with Deborah Lacks is the book's emotional core: a daughter trying to know the mother she lost as an infant, and a journalist trying to tell the story without repeating the exploitation she describes.
ideas.evidence: Skloot spent about a decade earning the family's trust, travelling with Deborah to Crownsville to recover Elsie's records; she set up the Henrietta Lacks Foundation to help the family and others.

key_claims_for_review.answer: A Black tobacco farmer from southern Virginia and mother of five whose cervical cancer cells, taken at Johns Hopkins in 1951, became the HeLa cell line.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: Why were HeLa cells scientifically important?
key_claims_for_review.answer: They were the first human cells to grow and divide indefinitely in culture, making them a standard tool for research across biology and medicine.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: Name two major uses of HeLa cells.
key_claims_for_review.answer: Testing the polio vaccine; research into cancer, viruses, gene mapping and in vitro fertilisation.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: Whose lab first grew HeLa cells?
key_claims_for_review.answer: George Gey's lab at Johns Hopkins.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: When and how did the Lacks family learn about HeLa?
key_claims_for_review.answer: In the 1970s, more than twenty years after Henrietta's death, when researchers contacted them for blood samples.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: What was the HeLa contamination problem?
key_claims_for_review.answer: HeLa cells were so vigorous that they had contaminated and overtaken many other cell lines, invalidating research based on them.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: What did Moore v. Regents of the University of California decide?
key_claims_for_review.answer: That a patient has no property rights over cells removed from his body, even when they are commercialised.

key_claims_for_review.prompt: What were the three strands of Skloot's book?
key_claims_for_review.answer: Henrietta's life and death, the scientific and commercial story of HeLa, and Skloot's relationship with the Lacks family.
